newsitem.title: UK: Continental Airlines demands squeeze on BA/American.
newsitem.headline: Continental Airlines demands squeeze on BA/American.

text.p: Continental Airlines Inc of the U.S. publicly voiced strong objections on Thursday to the British government's proposed conditions for allowing a controversial alliance between British Airways and American Airlines.

In comments to be submitted to Britain's competition advisory panel, the Office of Fair Trading, Continental said it alone would want 140 extra takeoff and landing slots per week at London's giant Heathrow airport to be able to compete.
The core British government proposal is that BA and American should be made to release a total of 168 weekly takeoff and landing slots at Heathrow airport for all competitors.
Last month the OFT asked other airlines participating in the market to submit their comments on the British government's proposals by January 10.

In a statement, Continental said it alone would require enough runway slots and facilties at the airport to operate at least six daily return flights between New York Newark and Heathrow -- "as well as the ability to add flights in response to competitive actions by the BA/American combine".
It would therefore be asking Britain to make available 140 weekly runway slots at Heathrow, along with "ample" appropriate facilities, the airline added.
Chairman Gordon Bethune called the alliance between BA and American effectively the world's largest airline merger.

"BA and AA promise to deliver the ultimate transportation benefit but, under a cold light and met with the full impact of ice-hard scrutiny, this huge deal is just as attractive to travellers as that last great wonder of the Altantic, The Titanic," he said.

Without tighter curbs, Continental said it believed the BA/American alliance would strangle competition on transatlantic routes by controlling more than 60 percent of all seats on the UK/U.S. market and more than 70 percent of seats from Heathrow to the United States.

"As a result, the OFT's proposed remedies would result in a far less competitive marketplace than air travellers enjoy today, even if one assumes an (Anglo-US) Open Skies (trade) agreement was struck," it added.

Earlier this week managers of another U.S. major, Delta Air Lines, said its general position would also be that the planned constraints were not restrictive enough to allow rivals to establish "meaningful competition" at Heathrow.
It did not give any more details of its position prior to meeting the OFT, however.
As well as other airlines, the U.S. government is also likely to have a say in the final form of any regulatory deal that clears the way for the alliance.

Washington has linked approval of the competition aspects of the deal to getting a so-called "open skies" agreement with Britain which would entail giving all U.S. airlines access to Heathrow -- Europe's most popular and lucrative hub for transatlantic air traffic.
